questions.text: Fresh concrete exerts pressure on vertical forms (walls, columns). This pressure is calculated as ___ (density × height) and increases with ___. Why does form pressure increase with concrete temperature?

options.text: ρg×h; depth. Warmer concrete sets faster, reducing hydrostatic-like pressure buildup. Higher temperature = earlier strength gain = lower form pressure required.
ρ/g×h; placement speed (faster placement increases pressure) due to the rapid accumulation of material weight
ρg/h; curing duration (longer curing increases pressure) as the concrete remains fluid for an extended period
ρ+g×h; admixture dosage (more admixtures increase pressure) by altering the mix's viscosity and setting time

rationale.c: Curing duration doesn't increase pressure; longer curing allows pressure reduction.
rationale.d: Admixture dosage (accelerators/retarders) affects set time, not directly pressure.
rationale.correct: Concrete form pressure ≈ ρg×h (weight density × gravity × fluid height). For vertical forms, max pressure occurs at depth. Warmer concrete (~30°C) sets faster than cool concrete (~10°C), so strength develops quicker, reducing time the concrete acts as a fluid. Result: lower peak pressure on forms. Placement rate also affects pressure—rapid placement maintains higher fluid height longer.

questions.explanation: ρ/g×h is dimensionally incorrect. Curing duration doesn't increase pressure; longer curing allows pressure reduction. Admixture dosage (accelerators/retarders) affects set time, not directly pressure. Concrete form pressure ≈ ρg×h (weight density × gravity × fluid height). For vertical forms, max pressure occurs at depth. Warmer concrete (~30°C) sets faster than cool concrete (~10°C), so strength develops quicker, reducing time the concrete acts as a fluid. Result: lower peak pressure on forms. Placement rate also affects pressure—rapid placement maintains higher fluid height longer.

questions.text: Conventional formwork uses ___ (coco lumber in Philippines) beams and joists supporting ___ decking, with ___ supporting the system at height.

options.text: timber; plywood; props (vertical supports)
steel panels; concrete; posts, which are typically used in more permanent structures
aluminum; OSB; jacks, often chosen for their lightweight and reusable properties
plastic; composite; anchors, which are less common in traditional formwork applications

rationale.b: Steel panels are system formwork, more expensive.
rationale.c: Aluminum/OSB is less common in Philippine practice; coco lumber dominates.
rationale.d: Plastic formwork is rare; timber is cost-effective.
rationale.correct: Conventional formwork: timber beams (coco lumber is economical in Philippines)/joists → plywood decking → props (vertical timber or steel columns) at base. Advantages: flexible, adaptable, low capital cost, reusable ~5–10 times. Standard in Philippine low-rise construction.

questions.explanation: Steel panels are system formwork, more expensive. Aluminum/OSB is less common in Philippine practice; coco lumber dominates. Plastic formwork is rare; timber is cost-effective. Conventional formwork: timber beams (coco lumber is economical in Philippines)/joists → plywood decking → props (vertical timber or steel columns) at base. Advantages: flexible, adaptable, low capital cost, reusable ~5–10 times. Standard in Philippine low-rise construction.

questions.text: Frame (Ringlock) scaffolding uses pre-fabricated ___ with integrated connections. Advantages: ___ assembly; disadvantages: ___.

options.text: frames; fast (training-free); less flexible than tube-and-clamp
tubes; slow (custom); highly flexible, allowing for complex configurations in irregular spaces
prefab towers; instant assembly; poor quality, often leading to frequent repairs and replacements
temporary structures; medium speed; unsafe due to lack of standardized safety features and inconsistent material quality

rationale.b: Tubes require clamp connections (manual); frames have integrated connections.
rationale.c: Prefab towers are specialized (not general scaffolding).
rationale.d: Frame scaffolding is established technology (not temporary/unsafe).
rationale.correct: Frame scaffolding: vertical and horizontal tubes slot into pre-welded frames. Ringlock systems allow vertical tubes to engage at any height. Advantages: rapid assembly (minutes per section vs. hours for tube-and-clamp), consistent design, minimal training. Disadvantages: higher capital cost, less flexible than tube-and-clamp (geometry must fit frame pitch/spacing).

questions.text: Philippine high-rise residential tower uses conventional coco lumber formwork with 7-day stripping cycle (70% strength assumption per ACI 347). During rainy season (June–October), site humidity exceeds 90% and ambient temperature drops to 20°C. How does this affect stripping schedule, and what corrective actions are needed?

options.text: Cool temperature (20°C) slows concrete strength gain vs. design assumption (25°C). Strength gain may take 10–12 days to reach 70%, not 7 days. Corrective actions: (1) Heat curing (heating blankets, steam) to accelerate; (2) Adjust stripping schedule to actual strength testing (break test samples at site); (3) Budget schedule buffer (3–5 days per floor) during rainy season. Moisture-saturated coco lumber also swells/warps; inspect carefully and consider protective covering.
Rainy season has no effect on concrete curing rate; stick to 7-day cycle, as the environmental conditions are considered negligible
High humidity accelerates curing; reduce to 5-day stripping, which is a common misconception without empirical support
Concrete strength is unaffected by temperature; only curing duration matters, which oversimplifies the complex interaction of factors

rationale.b: Cool temperature significantly slows strength gain; schedule must adjust.
rationale.c: High humidity slightly accelerates but does not overcome temperature reduction; net effect is slower strength gain.
rationale.d: Temperature directly affects cement hydration kinetics; it is the primary driver of strength gain rate.
rationale.correct: Concrete curing rate (strength gain) is temperature-dependent. At 20°C, strength gain is ~50% slower than at 25°C (design baseline). Design assumes 70% strength in 7 days at 25°C; at 20°C, achievement may take 10–12 days. Humidity (90%+) slows evaporation, which can accelerate curing slightly but not offset temperature reduction. Actions: (1) Heat curing (temporary enclosures, heating blankets, or infrared heaters) is the most practical—can maintain 25°C+ and reduce cycle to 7 days; (2) Strength testing (cylinder/beam break tests at site) provides definitive timing vs. assumptions; (3) Schedule buffer ensures no deadline pressure forces premature stripping. Wet coco lumber also warps/swells; protective covers/drying periods extend formwork reuse life.

questions.code_citation: ACI 347R-14; ACI 301; Philippine tropical construction practice

questions.text: A concrete slab was stripped at 5 days of curing (estimated ~50% strength per accelerated conditions). The slab shows mid-span deflection of 15 mm under self-weight and light construction loads. Is the slab acceptable, and what should be done?

options.text: The slab is non-compliant. Stripping at 50% strength is below ACI 347 minimum (70% for horizontal spans). Re-shoring/re-propping is required immediately to unload the slab and prevent further deflection/cracking. The slab has been damaged and may require structural repair or replacement.
15 mm deflection is acceptable; the slab is fine, which is a common assumption but may not consider long-term effects.
The slab is safe; deflection will recover after full curing (28 days), which is a hopeful but not guaranteed outcome.
Deflection is permanent but acceptable for short-span slabs, which may not meet all structural standards.

rationale.b: 15 mm deflection on a typical slab (~6 m span) is significant; permissible deflection is ~L/240 (typically 25 mm max, but damage occurs earlier).
rationale.c: Deflection does not recover; permanent creep and cracking remain.
rationale.d: Permanent deflection indicates damage; all slabs must meet serviceability criteria.
rationale.correct: ACI 347 specifies 70% minimum strength for horizontal span stripping. 5-day concrete at ~50% strength is insufficient. Deflection (15 mm) indicates over-stress; bending damage (micro-cracking) has occurred. Immediate action: re-prop the slab with shoring to unload it and stop further deflection. Once concrete reaches 70% strength (~7–10 days), reprops can be removed. Permanent deflection and internal cracking remain; structural capacity is permanently reduced. This failure is preventable by observing ACI 347 criteria.

questions.text: A formwork system is designed for concrete placement over 5 days, reaching 2.0 m height. Fresh concrete pressure is estimated at 2.4 kPa per meter depth, plus 15% impact factor, plus 2.4 kPa live load. At 3 m depth (during final placement day), calculate total pressure on the formwork.

options.text: Pressure = (2.4 kPa/m × 3.0 m × 1.15 impact) + 2.4 kPa live = (8.28 + 2.4) = 10.68 kPa total. Design formwork for 10.7 kPa minimum safety factor.
Pressure = 2.4 × 3.0 = 7.2 kPa (impact and live load ignored), which simplifies calculations but may underestimate actual conditions
Pressure = 2.4 × 2.0 = 4.8 kPa (maximum depth reached), assuming no additional loads are applied during the curing process
Pressure = 2.4 kPa only (live load negligible), which assumes that the live load does not significantly affect the formwork design

rationale.b: 2.0 m maximum is incorrect; formwork must support ongoing placement depth (up to 3.0 m in this scenario).
rationale.c: Impact and live load are significant; ignoring them underestimates design pressure by ~35%.
rationale.d: Only concrete pressure ignores impact and live load; design is unsafe.
rationale.correct: Calculation: Concrete pressure = 2.4 kPa/m × 3.0 m = 7.2 kPa. Impact factor (15%) adds: 7.2 × 0.15 = 1.08 kPa. Subtotal: 8.28 kPa. Live load (workers, tools, buckets): +2.4 kPa. Total: 10.68 kPa. Design formwork with safety factor (typically 1.5) → required capacity: 10.68 × 1.5 ≈ 16 kPa. Underestimating pressure causes formwork failure and concrete spillage.

questions.text: System (aluminum/steel panel) formwork reuses ___+ times and has ___–___ month capital amortization. It becomes economical for projects with ___ identical floors (typical high-rise).

rationale.b: 10 reuses is too low; capital cost not amortized.
rationale.c: 100 reuses is high; most projects max out at 30–50 cycles before technology obsolescence.
rationale.d: 3–5 floors is too few; capital remains unrecovered.
rationale.correct: System formwork: capital cost ~PHP 1–2 million for typical high-rise set. Reuse 50+ times amortizes capital when projects have 15+ floors using same panel dimensions. Amortization period: 12–36 months typical for continuous high-rise work. For fewer floors or custom geometry, conventional timber is more economical.

questions.text: Tube-and-clamp scaffolding uses ___ tubes connected by ___ (Manila clamps in Philippines). Advantages: ___ flexibility; disadvantages: ___ assembly.

options.text: steel tubes; clamps; high; labor-intensive
aluminum tubes; bolts; low; fast
wooden poles; rope; moderate; unsafe
prefab frames; welds; minimal; complex

rationale.b: Aluminum tubes are used; bolts are alternative to clamps.
rationale.c: Wooden poles with rope are unsafe (brittle failure).
rationale.correct: Tube-and-clamp: steel tubes (~40–50 mm diameter, locally ~3–4 cm in Philippines) connected by mechanical clamps (Manila clamps or proprietary). Advantages: highly flexible design, adaptable to irregular structures. Disadvantages: each connection requires manual tightening/inspection, slower assembly than frame systems, quality depends on clamp installation.

questions.text: ACI 347 specifies that formwork supporting horizontal spans (beams, slabs) must not be struck until concrete achieves approximately ___% of the design 28-day strength. Typical timeline: ___–___ days for normal Portland cement.

options.text: 90%; 21 days

rationale.b: 50% strength is adequate only for vertical members (columns); insufficient for horizontal spans.
rationale.c: 100% strength (28 days) is overly conservative; 70% is proven sufficient and reduces formwork cycle.
rationale.d: 90% strength exceeds requirements; 70% is the code standard.
rationale.correct: ACI 347R specifies 70% of f'c for horizontal spans. At 70% strength, concrete has sufficient bending capacity to support its self-weight plus live loads. Timeline: normal Portland cement achieves 70% strength in 7–14 days at ambient temperature (20–25°C). Accelerated curing (heat, steam, admixtures) reduces this to 1–3 days.

questions.text: OSHA Construction Standards 1926.500+ require ___ person certification, ___ inspection intervals, and ___ protection. Failure to comply exposes employers to ___.

options.text: competent; daily/weekly; fall protection (guardrails/harness); citations and fines; death liability
trained; monthly; basic helmets; warnings only, which may not adequately address safety concerns
certified; annually; no specific requirement; minimal penalties, potentially leading to insufficient safety measures
supervised; random; optional; educational notices, which may not enforce compliance effectively

rationale.b: Monthly inspection is insufficient; daily/weekly is required.
rationale.c: Basic helmets are insufficient without guardrails or harness.
rationale.d: Annual certification is inadequate; daily inspection is required.
rationale.correct: OSHA requires: (1) Competent Person (trained, certified) responsible for scaffolding design/inspection; (2) Daily/weekly documented inspections before occupancy; (3) Fall protection: guardrails (4 ft minimum), safety nets, or harness systems. Non-compliance: citations (serious violation: $9,000+), fines, work stoppage, and liability for injuries/deaths. Philippine DOLE enforces similar requirements per NSCP 2015 Chapter 34.
